items.title: I can describe an electron diffraction pattern and identify it as evidence for the wave-like nature of matter
items.what: When electrons are fired through a polycrystalline material such as graphite, they produce a pattern of concentric bright and dark rings on a screen. The bright rings are regions of constructive interference and the dark rings are regions of destructive interference.
items.why: The appearance of an interference pattern — a purely wave phenomenon — when using particles (electrons) is direct evidence that matter has wave-like properties, something Newton's classical mechanics cannot explain.
items.example: Electrons fired through a graphite target produce concentric bright and dark rings, similar in form to the X-ray diffraction pattern from the same material and to the circular diffraction pattern of laser light through a small circular aperture.

subtopic.name: Electron Diffraction and Wave-like Matter
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental evidence that electrons produce diffraction patterns when passed through crystalline materials, demonstrating wave-like behaviour. It also examines how electron diffraction patterns compare to those produced by X-ray photons.
subtopic.why: Electron diffraction was the first direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's hypothesis that matter has wave-like properties. Distinguishing electron and X-ray patterns is a key VCE skill for analysing evidence of wave-particle duality.

items.title: I can explain why the spacing of atomic layers in crystals makes them suitable for electron and X-ray diffraction
items.what: Diffraction is only significant when the wavelength is comparable to the gap size. Atomic layer spacings in crystals are on the order of 0.1 to 0.5 nm, which matches the wavelengths of both X-rays and electrons with typical laboratory energies.
items.why: Understanding this condition explains why crystals act as natural diffraction gratings for X-rays and electrons, and why visible light cannot be used to observe atomic structure through diffraction.
items.example: Graphite has an atomic layer spacing of 0.33 nm. An X-ray of wavelength 0.15 nm gives λ/w = 0.45, which satisfies the condition λ < w for observable diffraction. An electron with a de Broglie wavelength of 0.15 nm would produce an identical diffraction pattern from the same graphite.

subtopic.name: Electron Diffraction and Wave-like Matter
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental evidence that electrons produce diffraction patterns when passed through crystalline materials, demonstrating wave-like behaviour. It also examines how electron diffraction patterns compare to those produced by X-ray photons.
subtopic.why: Electron diffraction was the first direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's hypothesis that matter has wave-like properties. Distinguishing electron and X-ray patterns is a key VCE skill for analysing evidence of wave-particle duality.

items.title: I can distinguish between diffraction patterns produced by electrons and those produced by X-ray photons
items.what: Both electrons and X-rays produce similar ring-shaped diffraction patterns when passed through polycrystalline materials. The key difference is that applying a magnetic field deflects the electron beam (since electrons are charged) but does not affect X-rays. Also, changing electron speed changes the ring spacing, whereas X-ray ring spacing is unchanged by a magnetic field.
items.why: Being able to distinguish between electron and photon diffraction patterns is essential for correctly interpreting experimental evidence and for answering VCE questions that ask for the source of a diffraction pattern.
items.example: Two diffraction patterns are produced from the same graphite target: one by X-rays and one by electrons. If a magnetic field is applied and one beam deflects, that beam is the electron beam. If the electron speed is doubled, the rings become narrower because the de Broglie wavelength decreases.

subtopic.name: Electron Diffraction and Wave-like Matter
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental evidence that electrons produce diffraction patterns when passed through crystalline materials, demonstrating wave-like behaviour. It also examines how electron diffraction patterns compare to those produced by X-ray photons.
subtopic.why: Electron diffraction was the first direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's hypothesis that matter has wave-like properties. Distinguishing electron and X-ray patterns is a key VCE skill for analysing evidence of wave-particle duality.

items.title: I can state de Broglie's hypothesis that all matter has an associated wavelength
items.what: In 1924, de Broglie proposed that particles of matter have a wave-like nature, with a wavelength λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is the particle's momentum. This applies to all matter, but wave behaviour is only observable when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gap or obstacle.
items.why: This hypothesis unified the wave and particle descriptions of matter and was experimentally confirmed by Davisson and Germer in 1927 through electron diffraction, earning de Broglie the 1929 Nobel Prize.
items.example: An electron travelling at 4.9 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ has momentum p = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 4.9 × 10⁶ = 4.46 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹ and a de Broglie wavelength of λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 4.46 × 10⁻²⁴ = 0.15 nm, comparable to X-ray wavelengths used in crystal diffraction.

subtopic.name: The de Broglie Wavelength
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers de Broglie's proposal that all matter has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p, and the calculations required to find this wavelength for electrons, protons, neutrons, and other particles.
subtopic.why: The de Broglie wavelength connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter and is the foundation for understanding why electrons in atoms form stable standing wave states. It is also directly assessed in VCE numerical questions.

items.title: I can calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a particle using λ = h/p = h/mv
items.what: The de Broglie wavelength is calculated as λ = h/p, where p = mv for non-relativistic particles. Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s must be used (not the eV s form) when working with masses and velocities.
items.why: This calculation is directly assessed in VCE and is used to determine whether a particle will show measurable wave behaviour in a given experimental context.
items.example: A neutron of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg travelling at 2000 m s⁻¹: p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2000 = 3.34 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 3.34 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.199 nm.

subtopic.name: The de Broglie Wavelength
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers de Broglie's proposal that all matter has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p, and the calculations required to find this wavelength for electrons, protons, neutrons, and other particles.
subtopic.why: The de Broglie wavelength connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter and is the foundation for understanding why electrons in atoms form stable standing wave states. It is also directly assessed in VCE numerical questions.

items.title: I can explain why macroscopic objects do not show observable wave behaviour despite having a de Broglie wavelength
items.what: The de Broglie wavelength applies to all matter, but for large objects it is so small that diffraction effects are unmeasurably tiny. Measurable diffraction requires λ/w to be at least approximately 0.01.
items.why: This explains why quantum effects are only significant at atomic and subatomic scales, and why classical mechanics is sufficient for describing everyday objects.
items.example: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ has λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 20) = 2.2 × 10⁻³⁴ m. This is far smaller than even a proton (diameter ~10⁻¹⁵ m), making any diffraction completely undetectable.

subtopic.name: The de Broglie Wavelength
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers de Broglie's proposal that all matter has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p, and the calculations required to find this wavelength for electrons, protons, neutrons, and other particles.
subtopic.why: The de Broglie wavelength connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter and is the foundation for understanding why electrons in atoms form stable standing wave states. It is also directly assessed in VCE numerical questions.

items.title: I can describe the effect of increasing particle momentum on its de Broglie wavelength
items.what: Since λ = h/p, increasing a particle's momentum decreases its de Broglie wavelength, and decreasing momentum increases the wavelength. The relationship is an inverse proportionality.
items.why: This inverse relationship is important for predicting how changes in particle speed affect diffraction patterns: faster particles produce narrower diffraction patterns because their wavelength is shorter.
items.example: If the speed of electrons passing through a crystal is doubled, their momentum doubles and their de Broglie wavelength halves. The diffraction rings from the crystal will become narrower (smaller angular spread) because λ/w has decreased.

subtopic.name: The de Broglie Wavelength
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers de Broglie's proposal that all matter has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p, and the calculations required to find this wavelength for electrons, protons, neutrons, and other particles.
subtopic.why: The de Broglie wavelength connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter and is the foundation for understanding why electrons in atoms form stable standing wave states. It is also directly assessed in VCE numerical questions.

items.title: I can calculate the momentum of a photon using p = h/λ
items.what: Although photons have no rest mass, they carry momentum given by p = h/λ, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and λ is the photon's wavelength. This was predicted by Maxwell and confirmed experimentally by Compton.
items.why: Photon momentum explains physical phenomena such as radiation pressure on comet dust tails and solar sails, and it underpins the Compton effect in X-ray scattering.
items.example: A green photon with λ = 520 nm has momentum p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 520 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.28 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Photon Momentum
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the momentum carried by photons despite their zero rest mass, using the formula p = h/λ. It includes the comparison of photon and matter momentum for the same wavelength and applications such as radiation pressure.
subtopic.why: Photon momentum is the link between the wave and particle descriptions of light. It was confirmed by Compton's X-ray scattering experiments and is fundamental to understanding how light can exert forces on matter.

items.title: I can compare the momentum of a photon and a matter particle with the same de Broglie wavelength
items.what: Both photons and matter particles use the same formula λ = h/p, so if they have the same wavelength they have the same momentum. However, they differ in energy: a photon's energy is E = hc/λ, while a matter particle's kinetic energy is Ek = p²/2m.
items.why: This comparison highlights both the similarity (same wavelength means same momentum) and the difference (very different energies) between photons and matter particles, which is a key conceptual point in wave-particle duality.
items.example: A photon and an electron both have wavelength 0.42 nm, so both have momentum p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 0.42 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.58 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. The photon energy is E = hc/λ = 2.96 keV, but the electron kinetic energy is Ek = p²/2m = (1.58 × 10⁻²⁴)² / (2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.37 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = 8.6 eV — far less than the photon.

subtopic.name: Photon Momentum
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the momentum carried by photons despite their zero rest mass, using the formula p = h/λ. It includes the comparison of photon and matter momentum for the same wavelength and applications such as radiation pressure.
subtopic.why: Photon momentum is the link between the wave and particle descriptions of light. It was confirmed by Compton's X-ray scattering experiments and is fundamental to understanding how light can exert forces on matter.

items.title: I can apply conservation of momentum to a photon-electron collision
items.what: In Compton scattering, an X-ray photon collides with a loosely bound electron. Momentum is conserved, so the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after. The photon loses momentum (its wavelength increases) and the electron gains momentum.
items.why: Compton's experiment in 1923 provided direct evidence that photons carry momentum and that it is conserved in collisions, firmly establishing the particle-like nature of light.
items.example: A photon with momentum 6.6 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary electron, which recoils with momentum 1.1 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹ in the original direction. The remaining photon momentum is 6.6 × 10⁻²³ − 1.1 × 10⁻²² = −4.4 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹, meaning the photon has scattered in the opposite direction with magnitude 4.4 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Photon Momentum
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the momentum carried by photons despite their zero rest mass, using the formula p = h/λ. It includes the comparison of photon and matter momentum for the same wavelength and applications such as radiation pressure.
subtopic.why: Photon momentum is the link between the wave and particle descriptions of light. It was confirmed by Compton's X-ray scattering experiments and is fundamental to understanding how light can exert forces on matter.

items.title: I can explain how an emission line spectrum is produced in a gas discharge tube
items.what: When an electric current passes through a gas discharge tube, electrons collide with gas atoms and excite them into higher energy states. When these atoms decay back to lower states, they emit photons with energies equal to the difference between the energy states. This produces a spectrum of discrete bright lines at specific wavelengths.
items.why: Each element produces a unique emission line spectrum, which is used to identify elements both in the laboratory and in distant astronomical objects such as stars and exoplanet atmospheres.
items.example: Hydrogen gas in a discharge tube emits visible light at four specific wavelengths: 656.2 nm (red), 486.1 nm (blue-green), 434.0 nm (blue-violet), and 410.1 nm (violet). These correspond to electrons transitioning from higher states down to the n = 2 state.

subtopic.name: Emission and Absorption Spectra
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the production and interpretation of atomic emission line spectra and absorption line spectra, including those from gas discharge tubes and metal vapour lamps. It includes calculations of photon energy from spectral wavelengths.
subtopic.why: Line spectra are direct experimental evidence that atomic energy states are quantised. They also provide a practical tool for identifying elements in stars, comets, and exoplanet atmospheres — applications that link quantum physics to astrophysics.

items.title: I can explain how a metal vapour lamp produces an emission line spectrum
items.what: Metal vapour lamps use a hot electric arc to vaporise a metal such as sodium or mercury. The vaporised atoms are then excited by the current and decay, emitting photons at wavelengths characteristic of that metal's energy state transitions.
items.why: Metal vapour lamps are a practical application of atomic emission spectra and are commonly used in street lighting. Their characteristic colours (sodium yellow, mercury blue-white) are direct consequences of quantised energy states.
items.example: A sodium vapour lamp produces a distinctive yellow-orange glow dominated by two closely spaced lines near 589 nm, corresponding to transitions from the n = 2 excited state of sodium to the ground state.

subtopic.name: Emission and Absorption Spectra
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the production and interpretation of atomic emission line spectra and absorption line spectra, including those from gas discharge tubes and metal vapour lamps. It includes calculations of photon energy from spectral wavelengths.
subtopic.why: Line spectra are direct experimental evidence that atomic energy states are quantised. They also provide a practical tool for identifying elements in stars, comets, and exoplanet atmospheres — applications that link quantum physics to astrophysics.

items.title: I can explain how an absorption line spectrum is produced
items.what: When white light (continuous spectrum) passes through a cool gas, atoms in the gas absorb photons whose energy exactly matches the gap between two of their energy states. These photons are re-emitted in random directions, so the observer sees dark lines at those wavelengths against the continuous background.
items.why: Absorption spectra allow astronomers to identify elements in stellar atmospheres and the Sun's outer layers. The Fraunhofer lines in the solar spectrum are a well-known example of this phenomenon.
items.example: The solar spectrum contains a dark line at 656 nm. This corresponds to hydrogen atoms in the n = 2 state absorbing a 1.9 eV photon and transitioning to the n = 3 state. Because the re-emitted photons scatter in all directions, very few reach the observer, producing the dark line.

subtopic.name: Emission and Absorption Spectra
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the production and interpretation of atomic emission line spectra and absorption line spectra, including those from gas discharge tubes and metal vapour lamps. It includes calculations of photon energy from spectral wavelengths.
subtopic.why: Line spectra are direct experimental evidence that atomic energy states are quantised. They also provide a practical tool for identifying elements in stars, comets, and exoplanet atmospheres — applications that link quantum physics to astrophysics.

items.title: I can calculate the energy of an emitted or absorbed photon from its wavelength using ΔE = hf = hc/λ
items.what: The energy of a photon corresponding to a spectral line is calculated using ΔE = hf = hc/λ. This energy equals the difference between the two atomic energy states involved in the transition.
items.why: This calculation connects spectral observations directly to the quantised energy structure of atoms and is required for all numerical questions on energy state diagrams.
items.example: The shortest wavelength line in the helium emission spectrum shown in Figure 8B-8 is at 389 nm. Its energy is ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸) / (389 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.11 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.19 eV.

subtopic.name: Emission and Absorption Spectra
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the production and interpretation of atomic emission line spectra and absorption line spectra, including those from gas discharge tubes and metal vapour lamps. It includes calculations of photon energy from spectral wavelengths.
subtopic.why: Line spectra are direct experimental evidence that atomic energy states are quantised. They also provide a practical tool for identifying elements in stars, comets, and exoplanet atmospheres — applications that link quantum physics to astrophysics.

items.title: I can read an energy state diagram and identify the ground state, excited states, and ionisation energy
items.what: In an energy state diagram, the ground state (n = 1) is the lowest energy level. Excited states have higher energies labelled by quantum numbers n = 2, 3, 4, ... The ionisation energy is the energy required to completely remove an electron from the ground state.
items.why: Energy state diagrams are the standard tool for calculating photon energies, identifying transitions, and solving both emission and absorption spectrum problems in VCE.
items.example: In the hydrogen energy state diagram, the ground state is at 0 eV (or −13.6 eV in the alternative labelling). The n = 2 state is at 10.2 eV above the ground state. The ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV.

subtopic.name: Atomic Energy States
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the quantised energy states of atoms, how to read and use energy state diagrams, and how to calculate the energy and frequency of photons emitted or absorbed during transitions between states.
subtopic.why: Quantised energy states explain why atoms are stable, why they emit and absorb only specific wavelengths, and why classical physics fails at the atomic scale. This is the conceptual core of quantum physics as studied in VCE.

items.title: I can calculate the energy and frequency of a photon emitted or absorbed during a transition between two energy states
items.what: When an electron transitions from a higher state to a lower state, it emits a photon with energy ΔE equal to the difference between the two states. When it absorbs a photon, it transitions upward by the same energy. The frequency of the photon is found from f = ΔE/h.
items.why: This is the quantitative core of all energy state calculations and is directly assessed in VCE extended response and multiple choice questions involving emission and absorption spectra.
items.example: In hydrogen, the transition from n = 4 (12.8 eV) to n = 2 (10.2 eV) emits a photon of energy ΔE = 12.8 − 10.2 = 2.6 eV. Its frequency is f = 2.6 / (4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 6.28 × 10¹⁴ Hz, which falls in the visible (blue-green) range.

subtopic.name: Atomic Energy States
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the quantised energy states of atoms, how to read and use energy state diagrams, and how to calculate the energy and frequency of photons emitted or absorbed during transitions between states.
subtopic.why: Quantised energy states explain why atoms are stable, why they emit and absorb only specific wavelengths, and why classical physics fails at the atomic scale. This is the conceptual core of quantum physics as studied in VCE.

items.title: I can determine the number of different photon energies possible from transitions starting at a given energy state
items.what: From an excited state at quantum number n, an atom can transition to any lower state. The number of possible transitions (and therefore possible photon energies) from state n to the ground state is n − 1 direct transitions, plus all combinations of intermediate steps.
items.why: This is a common VCE question type. Being able to systematically list all possible transitions from a given state avoids missing photon energies in multi-step decay problems.
items.example: An atom excited to n = 4 can decay via: n=4→n=3, n=4→n=2, n=4→n=1, n=3→n=2, n=3→n=1, and n=2→n=1. That is six possible transitions and six possible photon energies from the hydrogen energy state diagram.

subtopic.name: Atomic Energy States
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the quantised energy states of atoms, how to read and use energy state diagrams, and how to calculate the energy and frequency of photons emitted or absorbed during transitions between states.
subtopic.why: Quantised energy states explain why atoms are stable, why they emit and absorb only specific wavelengths, and why classical physics fails at the atomic scale. This is the conceptual core of quantum physics as studied in VCE.

items.title: I can explain why classical physics fails to account for stable atomic energy states and why electron wave properties are needed
items.what: Classical physics predicts that an orbiting electron should continuously emit radiation and spiral into the nucleus, and that orbits should take a continuous range of energies. Neither prediction matches reality. The wave properties of electrons allow only certain standing wave states to be stable, producing quantised energy levels.
items.why: This is the conceptual reason why quantum mechanics was needed, and it links electron wave-particle duality directly to the structure of atoms and the existence of line spectra.
items.example: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, only orbits where the electron's de Broglie wavelength fits a whole number of times around the orbit circumference are stable. This produces discrete, stable energy states rather than the continuous spiral predicted by classical physics.

subtopic.name: Atomic Energy States
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the quantised energy states of atoms, how to read and use energy state diagrams, and how to calculate the energy and frequency of photons emitted or absorbed during transitions between states.
subtopic.why: Quantised energy states explain why atoms are stable, why they emit and absorb only specific wavelengths, and why classical physics fails at the atomic scale. This is the conceptual core of quantum physics as studied in VCE.

items.title: I can describe the result of a double slit experiment performed with single photons and explain what it reveals about the nature of light
items.what: When a double slit experiment is performed with light so dim that only one photon passes through the slits at a time, an interference pattern still builds up on the screen over many photons. This means each photon behaves as a wave and effectively passes through both slits simultaneously. However, if detectors are placed at the slits to determine which one the photon passes through, the interference pattern disappears and the photon behaves as a particle.
items.why: This experiment demonstrates that the wave and particle behaviours of light are mutually exclusive depending on whether a measurement is made. It is the clearest evidence for the dual nature of light.
items.example: With a very dim laser, the screen initially shows random dots. After thousands of photons, the familiar bright and dark bands of an interference pattern emerge — identical to the pattern produced by a bright laser — even though no two photons were present simultaneously to interfere with each other.

subtopic.name: Wave-Particle Duality
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the dual nature of both light and matter, using single-photon and single-electron double slit experiments as the key evidence. It also addresses the role of quantisation in the development of quantum physics.
subtopic.why: Wave-particle duality is the central conceptual challenge of quantum physics. The double slit experiments with single particles represent some of the most profound experimental results in physics and directly address the question of what light and matter fundamentally are.

items.title: I can describe the result of a double slit experiment performed with single electrons and explain what it reveals about the nature of matter
items.what: When electrons are sent through a double slit one at a time, an interference pattern builds up on the detector screen over time. If a measurement is made to determine which slit each electron passes through, the interference pattern disappears. This demonstrates that electrons, like photons, have both wave-like and particle-like properties.
items.why: The electron double slit experiment confirms that wave-particle duality is not unique to light — it applies to matter as well, extending the concept to all quantum particles.
items.example: In Roger Bach's 2013 experiment, one electron at a time was passed through a double slit. After 140,000 electrons, a clear interference pattern had formed on the detector, with the same bright and dark band spacing predicted by the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.

subtopic.name: Wave-Particle Duality
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the dual nature of both light and matter, using single-photon and single-electron double slit experiments as the key evidence. It also addresses the role of quantisation in the development of quantum physics.
subtopic.why: Wave-particle duality is the central conceptual challenge of quantum physics. The double slit experiments with single particles represent some of the most profound experimental results in physics and directly address the question of what light and matter fundamentally are.

items.title: I can explain the concept of wave-particle duality and apply it to both photons and electrons
items.what: Wave-particle duality means that both light and matter exhibit wave-like behaviour (diffraction, interference) and particle-like behaviour (discrete detection events, definite position when measured) depending on the experimental context. Neither model alone is sufficient.
items.why: Wave-particle duality is the foundation of quantum mechanics and explains phenomena ranging from atomic stability to the operation of electron microscopes and quantum computers.
items.example: A photon behaves as a wave when passing through a double slit (producing an interference pattern) but behaves as a particle when it is detected on the screen (producing a single localised dot). An electron similarly diffracts through a crystal lattice (wave behaviour) but is detected at a single location on a detector (particle behaviour).

subtopic.name: Wave-Particle Duality
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the dual nature of both light and matter, using single-photon and single-electron double slit experiments as the key evidence. It also addresses the role of quantisation in the development of quantum physics.
subtopic.why: Wave-particle duality is the central conceptual challenge of quantum physics. The double slit experiments with single particles represent some of the most profound experimental results in physics and directly address the question of what light and matter fundamentally are.

items.title: I can discuss the role of quantisation in the development of knowledge about light and the nature of atoms
items.what: Quantisation — the idea that physical quantities such as energy can only take discrete values — was introduced by Planck to explain blackbody radiation and extended by Einstein to explain the photoelectric effect. It was then found to apply to atomic energy states, explaining the stability of atoms and the existence of line spectra.
items.why: Recognising quantisation as a unifying idea across multiple phenomena (blackbody radiation, photoelectric effect, atomic spectra) is essential for understanding the historical and conceptual development of quantum physics as a VCE extended response skill.
items.example: Before quantisation, classical physics could not explain why atoms were stable or why they emitted only specific wavelengths of light. Einstein's quantisation of light energy into photons explained the photoelectric effect, and Bohr's quantisation of electron energy states explained hydrogen's line spectrum — both resolved major failures of classical physics.
